Aditya Hridayam

Stories from the Ramayana

Aditya Hridayam

Agastya teaches Rama the hymn to the Sun

In everyday English — Yuddha Kanda, sarga 105

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This book is the tale of a weary warrior — and a sage's teaching. Where there is weariness, read slowly; where the Sun's name comes, let light enter your voice.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Agastya calm and deep, Rama weary but firm.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, sarga 105 — the Aditya Hridayam. Rama has grown weary in the duel with Ravana — and then the sage Agastya comes. Anything more you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — prince of Ayodhya, fighting Ravana. Warm dark-brown skin, a calm and kind face, bow in hand, forest dress. In this book he is weary — but he does not give up.

Agastya — a great sage, white beard, saffron robes. He has come to watch the battle — and he teaches Rama the hymn to the Sun.

Surya — the Sun god, riding his golden chariot, the light and life of the world. The god of this hymn.

Ravana — king of Lanka. Tall, dark-complexioned, black moustache, tall golden crown, a single head, royal robes. In this book he is the enemy standing before Rama.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother, an archer, standing beside Rama.

Hanuman and Sugriva — chiefs of the vanara army, with Rama on the battlefield.

1 · The Weary Rama · · THE WEARY RAMA

On the battlefield before Lanka, a terrible duel was raging. Rama and Ravana — both on chariots, both with bows in hand — stood facing each other.

The battle had gone on for a very long time. Arrows rained down — chariots broke, bows broke, and new bows were taken up. Neither would step back.

Rama was weary. His arms felt heavy. Sweat stood on his brow. He stood holding his bow — looking at Ravana before him. Ravana too was weary — but he too stood his ground.

Lakshmana stood close by. Hanuman and Sugriva were watching too. In every heart there was one question — “What will happen now? When will this battle end?”

Rama closed his eyes — for a single moment. He thought — “I am weary. But I cannot stop. Sita is waiting. A righteous battle is never left unfinished.”

Rama said softly — “Lakshmana, the battle has grown long. But I will not step back.”

Lakshmana said — “Brother, we are with you. You are not alone.”

Pause and think — Rama is weary — but he is not defeated. Is being tired the same as being beaten? And when the body grows tired — where does the mind find its strength?

2 · Agastya Arrives · · AGASTYA ARRIVES

Then, at the edge of the battlefield, a sage arrived — Agastya. White beard, saffron robes, a calm walk. He had come to watch the battle — with the gods.

Agastya saw — Rama standing weary, bow in hand, looking toward Ravana. The sage smiled — he knew what Rama needed.

He came to Rama and said — “Rama, listen. I will tell you a secret — a hymn that will give you new strength.”

Agastya said — “Rama, this is the Aditya Hridayam — the hymn to the Sun. It is eternal, it is sacred — and it defeats the enemy. Learn it — and worship the Sun.”

Rama joined his hands and said — “Great sage, teach me. I am ready to listen.”

Agastya said — “First understand who the Sun is. Then take his names. Then chant. And see — how your weariness runs away.”

Pause and think — When someone is weary — what do they need most — rest — or a word that wakes the mind? Agastya does not give Rama rest — he gives him a hymn. Why?

3 · Who Is Surya · · WHO IS SURYA

Agastya said — “Rama, do not think of the Sun as only a disc in the sky. The Sun is the life of all beings.”

“The Sun is the one who rises in the morning — and the world wakes. The Sun makes the day day — and the night night. From the Sun's rays the grain ripens, the flowers bloom, and all living beings live.”

“The gods bow to the Sun — and the asuras too. For the Sun belongs to all — to the good and to the bad. He makes no distinction — he gives light to everyone.”

Agastya said — “One line of the hymn says — Rashmimantam samudyantam devasura-namaskritam — that is, the rayed one, rising, whom gods and asuras both bow to.”

Rama looked toward the Sun — the Sun shone in the sky — and its rays fell upon the battlefield.

Agastya said — “The Sun is the soul of all the gods. Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva — all are seen in the Sun. Whoever knows the Sun — knows them all.”

Pause and think — The Sun gives light to everyone — to the good and to the bad. Is that right? And is becoming like the Sun — doing good for all without distinction — the greatest strength of all?

4 · The Names of the Sun · · THE NAMES OF THE SUN

Agastya said — “Now hear the Sun's names. Every name tells one form of the Sun.”

“He is Aditya — the son of Aditi. He is Savita — the giver of birth to all. He is Surya — the giver of light to all. He is Khaga — the one who flies in the sky. He is Pushan — the nourisher of all.”

“He is Mitra — the friend of all. He is Varuna — the lord of the waters. He is Bhaskara — the maker of light. He is Vivasvan — the shining one. He is Bhuvaneshvara — the lord of the worlds.”

Agastya said — “The hymn says — Pujayasva Vivasvantam Bhaskaram Bhuvaneshvaram — that is, worship Vivasvan, worship Bhaskara — who is the lord of the worlds.”

“And another line says — Sarvadevatmako hyesha tejasvi rashmi-bhavanah — that is, he is the soul of all the gods, radiant, the maker of rays.”

“And hear this — Esha Brahma cha Vishnush cha Shivah Skandah Prajapatih — that is, he is Brahma, he is Vishnu, he is Shiva, he is Skanda and Prajapati. In the Sun, all the gods become one.”

Rama heard the names — and with every name his mind grew calmer. The weariness seemed slowly to lift away.

Pause and think — One Sun, and so many names — why? Does taking a name help us know someone better? And is speaking the name of someone dear, again and again — a way of remembering them?

5 · Chanting Thrice · · CHANTING THRICE

Agastya said — “Now chant, Rama. Look toward the Sun — and chant this hymn three times. Keep your mind calm — and hold the Sun in your heart.”

Rama looked toward the Sun. He joined his hands. And in his mind he chanted the Aditya Hridayam — once — then a second time — then a third time.

As he chanted, Rama's mind grew calm. The weariness lifted. It was as if the Sun's rays had entered within him — and his heart had filled with light.

Agastya said — “Now sip water three times — purify yourself with water — and take up your bow.”

Rama sipped water three times — and took up his bow. His face was no longer weary — it was shining.

The closing lines of the hymn say — Etach chhrutva mahateja nashta-shoko 'bhavat tada — that is, hearing this, the greatly radiant Rama's grief was destroyed. And — Adityam prekshya japtva tu param harsham avaptavan — that is, gazing at the Sun and chanting, he attained supreme joy.

Pause and think — Rama took up no new weapon — he only chanted a hymn. Does strength sometimes come not from outside — but from within? And does chanting three times mean — slowly, with the whole mind given to it?

6 · New Strength, New Resolve · · NEW STRENGTH, NEW RESOLVE

Rama took up his bow. His arms were no longer heavy. There was a new light in his eyes.

He looked toward Ravana — the same Ravana who a little while ago had seemed unconquerable — now he did not seem so great. In Rama's mind there was no fear — no grief.

Lakshmana said — “Brother, your face has changed!”

Rama smiled and said — “The sage Agastya has given me the Sun's hymn. Now I am ready.”

The sage Agastya blessed him — and went back with the gods. Rama moved toward the battle — toward the final duel with Ravana.

The hymn says — whoever chants it defeats the enemy, is freed from grief, and freed from fear. Rama had found all of this within himself.

But the final duel with Ravana — that story is in the next book.

Pause and think — Rama was weary — and a hymn gave him new strength. Are there words in our lives too — that lift us up when we are tired? And like the Sun — which rises again every morning — can we too begin again, every time?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main source

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, sarga 105 — Agastya teaching Rama the Aditya Hridayam.

The sarga number — 105 or 107?

In some editions this episode is found in sarga 107, and in others in sarga 105. The difference is only that different editions count the sargas a little differently — the story is the same. This book follows the main numbering, sarga 105.

About the hymn

The Aditya Hridayam has 31 verses. This book does not print the full Sanskrit text — it gives only the meaning of the hymn and a few short named lines, so that the story can be read. The full hymn can be read in the Ramayana itself.

Rama's weariness — the opening of sarga 105

Rama growing weary from the long battle, standing with his bow in hand, looking toward Ravana — this is at the opening of the sarga.

Agastya's arrival

The sage Agastya coming to the battlefield and teaching Rama the hymn — this is in the middle of the sarga. Agastya tells Rama that this hymn is eternal, sacred, and defeats the enemy.

Chanting thrice and taking up the bow

Rama chanting the hymn three times gazing at the Sun, sipping water three times, becoming pure, taking up his bow, and moving toward battle with joy — this is at the end of the sarga.

The fruit of the hymn

The hymn says that whoever chants it defeats the enemy, is freed from grief and from fear, and attains victory. In this book that fruit is told as a story — grief destroyed within Rama, and joy arriving.

What happens next

Rama is now ready for the final duel with Ravana. That battle — the slaying of Ravana — is in the next books of this series.
